opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For K2, I think the core priority was really agentic capability. We felt that the next stage of these models isn't just about chatting well or answering a single question; it's about whether the model can actually take actions, use tools, work through a long multi-step task, and get something done in a real environment. So a lot of the design decisions flowed from that goal.

The second thing was token efficiency. High-quality pretraining data is growing much more slowly than compute, so the question becomes how much intelligence you can extract from each token you have. That's part of why we put a lot of effort into the optimizer side, using Muon at scale and working on making it stable, with what we call MuonClip, so we could train a very large model smoothly without loss spikes. That stability matters a lot when you're spending that much compute on one run.

Architecturally, we went with a large mixture-of-experts model, with a very large total parameter count but a relatively small number of activated parameters. That gives you a lot of capacity while keeping inference cost reasonable, which matters if you want people to actually use the model for long agentic tasks.

On the post-training side, we invested heavily in synthesizing agentic data, building many tool-use environments and trajectories at scale, and then using reinforcement learning, including on tasks where the reward isn't easily verifiable. The aim was a model that's useful in practice, not just good on benchmarks.

And finally, we chose to open-source it. We think putting a strong base and a strong agentic model out there helps the whole ecosystem move faster, and it also pushes us to keep raising the bar ourselves.

fable-5.1.text:
With K2, the first thing we decided was that we were not going to spend a trillion parameters chasing a trillion-parameter number. We'd been tracking the problem for a long time, and the thing that kept coming back was token efficiency. You have a finite supply of high-quality tokens in the world, and the question is how much intelligence you can extract from each one. That reframes almost everything. Scale still matters, but the scaling you care about is intelligence per token, not just raw compute.

That's why so much of our effort went into the optimizer and training stability. If you're going to train a very large sparse model on a fixed token budget, you cannot afford loss spikes and you cannot afford to leave signal on the table. We spent a lot of time on MuonClip precisely because Muon gave us better sample efficiency, but at that scale it would blow up attention logits. So we built the clipping mechanism around it, and the whole pretraining ran without a single spike. That sounds like an engineering detail, but it's really a design priority: we chose to bet on a newer optimizer because token efficiency was the thing we valued most.

The second priority was agentic capability. We had a strong view that the next stage isn't a model that answers well, it's a model that acts well over long horizons, using tools, recovering from mistakes. You can't get that from pretraining data, because it basically doesn't exist on the internet in any volume. So we built large-scale synthetic environments and tool-use pipelines, thousands of tools, real and simulated, and trained the model to complete multi-step tasks in them. And then reinforcement learning on top, with verifiable rewards where we could get them and a self-critic rubric where we couldn't. The point was to let the model learn from its own experience, because that's where you get the data that pretraining can't give you.

The third one was openness. We released the base model and the instruct model open-weight, which was a real decision rather than an afterthought. Partly it's about trust and distribution, but partly it's because we think a model like this becomes more useful when the community builds on it and finds things we didn't anticipate.

And I'd say underneath all of that is a bias toward simplicity. We made the model non-thinking by default, very large but with a modest number of active parameters, so it's efficient to serve. We didn't want cleverness for its own sake. We wanted a foundation that is stable, efficient, good at using tools, and that people can actually run and extend. That was K2.

astra-6.text:
The central priority was usefulness: could the model help someone carry a task through to completion? That means thinking about reasoning, coding, and tool use together, rather than treating them as isolated capabilities. A model needs to understand the goal, take an appropriate action, and use the result to decide what to do next.

The other priority was efficiency. Strong capabilities matter, but so does the cost of putting them into practice. So the design challenge was to improve what the model could accomplish while keeping it practical to use.

sol-6.1.text:
The main priority was to make the model useful for solving real problems. That means looking beyond whether it can give a good answer to a single question: can it understand a complicated task, reason through the steps, use tools when needed, and carry the work through to completion?

We also wanted to balance capability with efficiency. Intelligence matters, but so does the cost of putting it into practice. And reliability is essential—recognizing uncertainty, following instructions, and producing results people can actually use.
